['In answer to that question, I may say that, had I been here I would have voted against that proposal, not so much because I considered it unfair in itself, but on account of its being sprung by surprise on the people. I am not called upon to discuss that question just now; I have referred to it by the way and not with any idea of criticism. It seems to me that in connection with questions of such importance, it would be advisable to consult the people. The manner of consulting the people which the government have adopted is not the ideal one to my mind. It is in accordance neither with the spirit nor with the letter of the constitution. It is an arbitrary and antiliberal mode of procedure; it is neither generous nor frank, and surely it is not manly.
That sovereign people in whose presence, during the elections, politicians are so apt to take a cringing attitude, is deserving of more consideration.
As will have been noticed, the extra expenditure on this undertaking will be enormous. As stated by the ' Witness ' that road will entail on the Dominion an expenditure, not of thirteen millions, not of a hundred millions, but rather of $250,000,000 or possibly $280,000,000. This government is going to supply all the funds for this undertaking from Moncton to Prince Rupert, from ocean to ocean, for all sections east and west, and the prairie and mountain sub-sections, including the Quebec bridge, and these amounts will be returned when there are funds available.
With whom are we dealing? Is it with the Grand Trunk Pacific, or with the Grand Trunk Company of Canada, or with a third company which has made its appearance under the name of the Grand Trunk Town Site and Development Company; or lastly, is it with the fourth company, the "Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Line Company"? All these companies are apparently amalgamated ; the directors are the same in every case, they constitute in reality a single moral person; and I say that parliament should under the circumstances show great caution in granting them favours. They are endeavouring to secure privileges, while avoiding all risks. These companies are much more anxious to make money out of us than to endure the welfare of the country.
The hon. Minister of Railways stated a minute ago how important it was from our point of view to have an entirely Canadian line of railway, over an all-Canadin route. Now, do all these companies which seem so anxious to provide us with an all-Canadian Mr. ETHIER.
Transcontinental Railway, have as stock holders and directors Canadian citizens, oi at any rate foreigners intending to become citizens of Canada. Are they not rather strangers, Americans, anxious to make money at our expense, without even going to the length of getting naturalized?
When I heard the Minister of Railways and his friends booming the West, I remember what the Liberals had to say in this connection in 1880 and 1884. It is important, I think, to recall the past, for fear certain incidents in the history of our country should be too soon consigned to oblivion. It was not usual then to boom the West, to speak of it as destined to become the world's great storehouse. I shall quote presently some of the sayings of these gentlemen in that connection, when the Canadian Pacific Railway was applying to parliament for help towards the completion of their undertaking.
However, as regards this proposed second transcontinental, it was launched prematurely, with inexplicable haste, in the full blast of a session, when parliament was drawing to an end, and against all expectations. It should be no matter for surprise if in the end the expenditure is found to be enormous. Arrangements were taken as if the matter had been of very little importance, without going to the pains of getting precise information in regard to the physical features of the country through which the railway was to be built, nor as regards the expenditure, and the cost of the road in stead of amounting to $13,000 per mile or $30,000 per mile, reaches $35,000 and even $80,000 per mile.
That is not surprising; it was bound to happen, and the best evidence of it I find in a speech of the right hon. Prime Minister, delivered on July 30th, 1903. He said:
I do not expect even the most fastidious of our critics will ask us that we should have had an exploration across the prairies. They are satisfied that we have enough information now to deal with this question so far as the prairies are concerned. But I shall be asked: What about the Rocky mountains? My answer in regard to the Rocky mountains is that we have mountains of information. We have mountains of books, pamphlets and reports-books, pamphlets and reports from traders, from explorers, from engineers.
And he mentioned Samuel de Champlain, Robert Cavelier de la Salle, La Verendyre, Alexander Mackenzie, Captain Butler and many others who at that early date, in their travels on land and sea, had not the least idea of making surveys or specifications and estimates for railways. No wonder that with such data, the government should have been out in their calculations.

Mr. FIELDING moved second reading ol Bill (No. 128) to authorize a loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Before the Bill passes, I would like to address a few observations to the House respecting the position of this matter as it stands, having re-

gard to the debate which has already taken place on the resolution. A good many things have happened since the 30th of July, 1903, when the right hon. the Prime Minister delivered, on the first reading, of the Bill, a very lengthy address covering about forty columns of ' Hansard,' without doing us the courtesy of sending us an advance copy of the Bill, but contenting himself with presenting to us, at the conclusion of the speech, a copy of the Bill which, of course, we had no opportunity of examining or considering at that stage before replying to that speech. The Tight hon. gentleman indulged on that occasion in a great many predictions-predictions with regard to the outcome of the enterprise and predictions with regard to its cost ; and it is said that this particular enterprise is to be regarded as his special political monument. Well, I have only to say that if any monument should be erected in this connection, I would suggest that it ought to be in duplicate-one containing the predictions as to cost, should be erected at Moncton ; and the other, giving the actual cost, at Prince Rupert, so that no one could see the two except at very considerable intervals of distance and time.
, When one comes to consider five years later that we were solemnly told in the first place that this government possessed mountains of information, the most absolute and accurate information that could be desired -I presume that is what that term was intended to express-not only with regard to the merits of the enterprise when once completed, but with regard to the cost of that enterprise, one is amazed at the discrepancy between the predictions based on this absolute information and the results which have obtained thus far. When we contrast the solemn statement made to the House upon those mountains of information, upon the reputation and knowledge of the Prime Minister of Canada, that the mountain section would cost $18.000,000-when we contrast that with the latest report of the officer of this government, charged with the supervision of the western division, who informed the House and country that the same mountain division, instead of costing $18,000,000, will cost $67,000,000, we are reminded of the works of a celebrated German thinker and writer :	' Nothing is so terrible as ignorance in action.'
Now, Mr. Speaker, the project of constructing a transcontinental railway across this country is a very great enterprise, and I thoroughly understand that the people of Canada ought not to be backward in dealing with the great problem of transportation, whether in the east or west of Canada, or whether covering Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. But there are some people in this country who seem to take it for granted that any great railway corporation entering upon an enterprise of this

kind has an absolute vested right to all the assistance that the resources of this country can give. I do not so regard the situation. It may be very much in the interest of the people of this country, as sometimes it has been in their interest in the past, that public assistance should be given to great schemes of transportation. That was done in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It has been done in the case of the Canadian Northern. And last, but not least, it has been done in connection with the enterprise we are now discussing. But it is not too late, it seems to me, to emphasize once more the importance of the statement made to the House by the Prime Minister, in 1903, and again in 1904, namely, that the Grand Trunk Railway Companv were in this enterprise and were of it and formed the whole thing ; and the proposal which confronts the people of Canada to-day is that the same Grand Trunk Railway Company being in this enterprise and of it and forming the whole thing, are asking the people of Canada to hand back to them $7,000,000, which they have invested in it. Well, it may even be in the interests of the country to do this, although it .is a rather stiff propositon, considering what was promised and declared to us in 1903-4 -it may be in the interests of the country to do that rather than allow this work to stop, and the credit, not only of this company, but of Canada as a whole, to be thereby affected; but I desire, before the Bill is read the second time, to point out that not only is the Grand Trunk Pacific in difficulties over this enterprise, but that, looking a little ahead into the future and having Tegard to the terms of this bargain, we can very readily foretell that the government itself will be in difficulties over it before long. One of my objects in speaking on the second reading of this Bill, before it goes to committee, is to point out what I deem some of these difficulties to be, and to inquire from the government whether or not they have had these under consideration and whether or not they propose, or have proposed, to arrive at any understanding or agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company for the purpose of preventing certain unfortunate consequences to this country that, it seems to me, are very likely to occur.
I have already emphasized the probable cost of this road. Roughly speaking, from the best information I can gather from the utterances of hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches themselves, the entire road will cost in the vicinity of $300,000,000. The eastern division will cost at least $180,000,000, and probably $190,000,000, all of which must be paid out of the revenues of Canada. The western division will cost *-if my estimates are correct-and I have based them on information afforded by the
government itself, between $110,000,000 and $120,000,000. And if you look for a moment at the details of the expenditure,, you will find about this result. The government provides in cash, in respect of interest on the mountain section-interest paid by the people of this country without any recourse-$13,413,750; the government provides in guarantees and bonds for both the prairie and mountain sections $66,658,000; then there is the loan now proposed of $10,000,000. If you sum these up, you will find the total to be $90,101,750, and you will find also that the Grand Trunk Railway will guarantee bonds, according to the information brought down by the government, to the extent of about $28,750,000.
Now, it must be obvious to any person, that the only real security we have for this loan and these guarantees will be the success of the enterprise. If the enterprise is not successful, we have no real security; if the enterprise is successful we shall have good security. So far_ as I am concerned, I have no hesitation in saying that it is my sincere hope that the enterprise will ultimately be successful. But in the meantime, if there be any risk-and n,o one can say, in a great enterprise of this kind there is not some risk at least- we are assuming about nine-tenths of that risk and the Grand Trunk Railway about one-tenth. Now, the road, it is needless to remind hon. gentlemen on both sides, is being built out of moneys derived from two sources. The greater part of the money for the building of the road was provided by the people of Canada, or upon their credit, and the remainder by the influence and financial support of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. If you consider this as one great railway enterprise, one Transcontinental Railway extending from Moncton in New Brusnwick to Prince Rupert in British Columbia, the country is financing this enterprise to the extent of nine-tenths and the Grand Trunk Railway Company is financing it to the extent of one-tenth. Now what advantage and what benefit do the people of this country as represented by the government receive on the one hand and what does the Grand Trunk Railway on the other hand, receive from the enterprise? I am not speaking for the moment of the benefit that may accrue to the people of this country from having a great line of transportation extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I do not overlook that, nor do I desire to minimize it. But, looking at the direct financial advantage and results which can be derived from this railway enterprise, you will observe that the Grand Trunk Railway, in return for the financial support and backing which it is giving to this enterprise, is receiving-nay, has

already received-common stock of this company to the amount of $25,000,000, common stock handed over otherwise for a mere nominal consideration. You do not find the people of Canada, who have given their financial support to this enterprise to the extent of nine-tenths of the money necessary for the building of the whole line, in this regard at least you dp not find them receiving a single dollar of profit from this enterprise-not a single dollar is Canada to receive of the great future profits which will accrue from the operation of this road if it proves successful, as we all hope it may, not only in the distant but in the immediate future. Now, is there any _ particular reason why a result of that kind should accrue from this proposition? Has the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway corporation, or any other corporation in Canada any vested right to government assistance for the purpose of building a road through the very best portion of Canada so that, although it receives such splendid, such enormous financial support as that just being given by the people of this country to the enterprise of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, they shall receive $25,000,000 of common stock, and the people of Canada represented by this government shall receive absolutely no return or compensation of that kind ?
Mr. Speaker, we did make an argument in 1904 and we proposed a resolution in that respect from which I, for one, do not recede to-day. I think that if our proposition had been accepted by the government it would have resulted in very much greater benefit to the people of this country than any which is likely to accrue to them from the proposition as carried out. We said in 1904 that as the people of Canada were providing nine-tenths of the financial support necessary to construct this great transcontinental railway there was every reason for believing that the wise course would be to go one step further and provide ten-tenths instead of nine-tenths and	own the
road from the Atlantic to the Pacific as a great national highway in every sense of the term. I, for one, have never been able to appreciate the arguments of the government in that regard. I should not dignify what was said in opposition to that proposal by the name of argument, because, speaking in all sincerity from my place in this House, I have never heard anything from the other side in opposition to the proposal which deserved the name of argument. If you are pledging your credit or handing over your money for the construction of a great public utility what especially is the object in handing that public utility over to a railway corporation ? I am distinguishing sharply, just now, between government ownership and government operation. I am bound to admit that government operation of the Intercolonial has not Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
been very successful, and I do not think we have had, in the past ten years especially, any such object lessons from the operation of the Intercolonial as would suggest that we should move forward along that line until we have demonstrated-as I believe we can demonstrate-that the Intercolonial Railway or any other state-owned railway in Canada can be operated as economically and efficiently as any corporation-owned road in this country or any other. We have not done so up to the present time. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals proposes to take some steps which he believes may result in important advances and benefits, and I sincerely hope and trust that his expectation may be fuilly realized.
But reverting for a moment to the argument on the point I have just suggested, why should you hand over a great public utility that we have paid for? Why should the government, in 1904, have desired to do that? Is it in the interest of the people of this country that we should hand over all our forests to a private corporation, formed for speculative purposes or for operating purposes? Is it desirable that we should hand over all our water-powers? Is it desirable that we should hand over all our mines and minerals? Is not the true course, the wise oolicy rather that which is being pursued by the provincial government of Ontario, when it retains its forest wealtli and its mineral wealth under such conditions that royalties, bonuses and rentals should be received proportionate to the increasing value of that public domain, as it does increase in value year after year? So it does not seem to me the height of wisdom, to say the least, that the government of this country should have pledged the country's credit, as they did pledge that credit in 1903 and 1904, to almost the whole extent necessary to build this great transcontinental railway, merely for the purpose of handing it over to a private corporation, and so that such private corporation shall enjoy all the fruits, advantages and benefits which may result from the- increasing value of that road, when the great west of Canada has a population of 10,000,000, 15,000,000 or perhaps 25,000,000 people. Well, that contract has been made, we cannot undo it now except with the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company; and I presume it would be rather too much to expect that either one or the other of those companies would be willing to consent to a proposal of that kind.
But it does not seem to me to be too late,
when we come to some other considerations, for the government to have regard to the true interest of the people. There are $20, 000,000 of preferred stock of the Grand

Trunk Pacific Company still. If we are to finance this road to the further extent of $10,000,000, would it be absolutely out of the question that we should say to the Grand Trunk- Pacific Kailway Company. 'Very good, hand us over $10,000,000 of that preference stock, and we will be very glad indeed to assist this enterprise, because we thoroughly realize the misfortune which would be entailed, not only upon the company but upon the people of this country, if any stoppage should occur in that work.' Let us look at it for a moment. The Grand Trunk Company finances the road to the extent of one-tenth of its total cost, receiving $25,000,000 of common stock. The people of this country finance this road tc the extent of nine-tenths of its total cost, to the extent of $275,000,000. Would it be too audacious, would it be trenching too much upon the rights and privileges of railway promoters in this country, if the government of Canada should at this juncture say, 'You are receiving $25,000,000 of common stock for financing this road to the extent of one-tenth of its cost; give us $10,000,000 of preference stock for financing this road to the extent of the remaining nine-tenths of the total cost. Has the government made any proposal of that kind to the Grand Trunk Railway Company? If not, are they absolutely oblivious of what the true interests of the people are?
My hon. friend has spoken during this session of the land grant to the Canadian Pacific Kailway Company. Does he doubt that the men who were at the back of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at that time, would have taken 75 cents per acre for that land, and been glad to get it in those days? I have it on the best information that they would have been ready and willing to compound their land grant of 25.000,000 acres at 75 cents on the dollar. Why was the land valueless at that time? Because of its inaccessibility. What makes that land valuable at the present time? The building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, founded mainly upon the faith, hope, courage, and foresight of the great statesmen of those days, who realized what the splendid future of that great western country was going to be.
Then it seems to me that there are some other considerations the government might very well have had in mind. I will not allude to all of them just now, because it would be better perhaps that some of those subjects should be adverted to in committee. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance considers this is a banking transaction. If it is to be regarded as a banking transaction, and if we are to take the ground that a government, in conducting a banking transaction with a great railway enterprise of this kind, should make
no profit, at least the government ought to keep the people whole; we ought not surely to loan money to the Grand Trunk Pacific at a lower rate of interest than that which we have to pay.
But there is another matter, and I alluded to it in a question which I addressed to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways a day or two ago. I would like to know whether the government has taken into consideration what its position will be with respect to the line from Quebec to Moncton before the completion of the Quebec bridge. In the first place I would like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals whether he is prepared to set any date upon which that bridge is likely to be completed?

In reply to my hon. friend, it is impossible to do that until the board have fully completed their plans and have reported them. We have not interfered with them in any way, as we want to put upon them the full responsibility of getting a complete set of plans for the bridge, the building and permanency of which will be absolutely assured. I hope the time will come when we can give that information, but at the present moment I am not able to do so.
Could not the hon. gentleman state an approximate date?
No.

Then I am without any information from the government. But I have been informed by an authority for which I have some respect, that the very earliest date at which that bridge can be completed would be 1915 or 1916. I am informed further-and the Minister of Railways will correct me if I am wrong, because it is a matter of which I have no personal knowledge-I am informed further that the line from Quebec to Moncton will be completed in 1910; so there you will have a period of five ot six years at least during which the line from Moncton to Quebec will be upon the hands of the government. The estimates already brought down show that that road will cost about $29,000,000. I am informed on authority for which I have a good deal of regard, that that road will probably cost well up to $35,000,000 before it is completed. But I am not going to argue on that assumption. I will assume that the road will cost $30,000,000. I would ask the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) or the Prime Minister whether they have at present any idea as to what they would do with the road during that period?

My hon. friend can clearly understand that the conditions which have arisen were entirely and wholly unexpected, that they have to be treated

as unexpected conditions and cannot very well be criticised from the standpoint of a premeditated arrangement of the government or the country. Conditions having arisen which are wholly unexpected, the government have under consideration the establishment, if it be possible, of a ferry across the river at that point. My hon. friend smiles. Possibly from a practical standpoint he has a right to smile, as he understands some of the difficulties that would ensue.
I was not smiling.
I would not at all complain if he did smile.

I thoroughly realize that the government did not anticipate the fall of the Quebec bridge. I do not want my hon. friend to imagine that I do not appreciate the fact that this situation is entirely unexpected. The fact that it is unexpected has left the government face to face with a certain condition, and I think the House ought to be made acquainted with the proposals of the government in this connection, because, while the Grand Trunk Pacific Company is in difficulties with respect to the financing of the prairie section, this government is also in difficulties with respect to the operation of that road for five or six years between Quebec and Moncton. Therefore, when one party to the contract, being in a certain difficulty, comes to the other party to the contract, also in a very considerable difficulty, it might have been regarded as a matter of reasonable prudence that both difficulties should have been considered at the same time and that some arrangement should have been made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to lift the government out of the difficulty occasioned by the fall of the Quebec bridge. Has the Minister of Railways and Canals made any estimate of what percentage the interest and depreciation upon the line from Quebec to Moncton will amount to per annum?
I have not.

I 'am unable to get any information from my hon. friends opposite, but I have endeavoured to obtain some information from outside, and I am informed, upon authority for which I have a good deal of respect, that the interest and depreciation upon that road during those five years will amount to at least 7 per cent ner annum, in other words $2,100,000 per annum, or, if you estimate a period of five years, $10,500,000. This country has great resources, but still a condition which involves an amount of that kind during a period of five years might, it seems to me, invite the attention even of my right hon. friend who claims that his soul is turned to higher things than considerations of this kind.

Then I would like to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals, and I am giving him this notice now in order that we may discuss the matter in committee upon the most ample notice, whether or not he imagines that that line from Winnipeg to Moncton, with a ferry across the St. Lawrence river, can be operated as a through line, for the transportation of wheat for example? I have no knowledge upon that subject except that which comes to me from persons who, as I think, are qualified to judge, and they entertain a very great doubt unon the subject, in fact they are rather inclined to laush at the idea. Would the minister propose to operate his ferry there during the winter? Has he undertaken to consider the expense of that? Does he remember the language to which we listened from a certain hon. gentleman in this House put up by the government in the debates of 1903 and 1904 as their great authority upon this subject? Does he remember that Mr. Charlton, the gentleman to whom I refer, spoke of trains a mile long, hauled over grades not exceeding four-tenths of one per cent, trains which, according to his estimation, would be able to haul grain from Winnipeg to Quebec in competition with water carriage? Does he imagine that these trains a mile long, going over grades of that kind from Winnipeg to Quebec, can be transported across the St. Lawrence in winter and go on to Moncton, and that all this can be done upon a profitable basis according to the view placed before the people of Canada in some of the glowing speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite in 1903 and 1904?
Then there is another consideration. What about the local traffic on the line from Quebec to Moncton? Has my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) any information which would indicate that the local traffic upon that line can be of any appreciable value considering the enormous cost of the road between those two points? If he has any information of that kind I can only say it is entirely dissimilar to any information I have been able to collect from authorities to whom I have applied for information on this subject.
Another consideration in connection with the line from Quebec to Moncton concerns the operation of the road not only before but after the Quebec bridge shall have been built. I gave the government credit, when I spoke on this subject during the *present session, for a saving of 29 miles in distance between Quebec and Moncton as compared with the Intercolonial Railway. That was on the government's statement and I am bound to assume that it is a correct statement; if there is any variation from it later on, it will be a matter for criticism. In the debate of 1903, the government claimed that the Intercolonial Rail-

way was wholly unsuitable lor transcontinental traffic on account of its excessive grades. Mr. Charlton, who was put up to reply to the criticism of the late Mr. Blair, elaborated this point very fully, as may be seen by any gentleman who will refer to page 8481 of 'Hansard' of 1903. That gentleman then said:
What are the grades on the Intercolonial
Railway? There are 62J feet grades, and 50 foot grades to the mile. No road can claim lo be a first-class road with grades more than cne-half per cent or 26 feet to the mile. In the construction of this short line

Because at that time you will remember the Prime Minister estimated that there would be a saving of at least 120 miles in the distance between Quebec and Moncton.
-in the construction of this short line and in the construction of the line from Quebec to Winnipeg it should he an absolute condition that the road should be first-class in point of grades, in point of construction and ih point of weight of rails. The object of the building of a short line from Chau-diere Junction to Moncton is to correct the costly mistake that the country made when
the Intercolonial Railway was constructed____
Why should we shorten, straighten and improve the Intercolonial Railway? It is simply because we have set out with the purpose of securing trade for our own seaports, and if we are to secure that trade we must have the best obtainable conditions with regard to our lines of transportation. We must not have to go away around by the sea 120 miles further than a short line would take us. We must not have grades 62J feet to the mile, but we must reduce the distance, reduce the grades, improve the efficiency of the road and secure the necessary conditions so far as it is possible to do so in order to get the trade. That, we aim to get.
Now, I understand that the government has obtained this advantage of 29 miles in distance by the adoption of what are called pusher grades. In that connection it is not out of place that I should give to the House what information I have as to the grades of both the Intercolonial Railway and the National Transcontinental Railway between Quebec and Moncton. The Intercolonial Railway follows the St. Lawrence for some two hundred miles east of Quebec to St. Flavie and while it is true it has grades of one per cent at a few points in this distance a large proportion of the two hundred miles is comparatively level road.
From St. Flavie on the St. Lawrence it crosses the summit between the Quebec and New Brunswick waters at an elevation of 751 feet above sea level or 485 feet above St. Flavie and 25 miles in distance therefrom. For the next 150 miles to Gloucester Junction the line follows the Metapedia lake, the Metapedia river and the Bay Chaleur and the grades are exceedingly favourable.
For the next 117 miles to Moncton the line runs nearly at right angles to the river and consequently the grades are not so favourable. There is one summit of 500 feet between Bathurst and Newcastle and three others of about 300 feet each between Newcastle and Moncton.
The National Transcontinental Railway begins to rise directly after leaving Quebec and steadily climbs for about 105 miles to a summit of between 1,400 and 1,500 feet above sea level and then drops 1,000 feet, in the next one hundred and ten miles to Edmundston on the St. John river in New Brunswick, to within 470 feet of sea level.
Then it rises and falls and passes over some considerable summits for about 100 miles when it reaches the Tobique river at an elevation of about 500 feet above sea level. From that point it rises almost continuously to an elevation of about 1,400 feet above sea level at the head waters of the Miramichi river, a distance of 116 miles F. Then it falls about 1,300 feet in 100-miles to an elevation of 100 feet above sea level at the crossing of the Salmon river at Chipman.
From Chipman to Moncton, 56 miles, there are no high summits to cross and altogether the grades on this section are favourable.
In the net result, so far as^ the National Transcontinental Railway is , concerned, there are at least two pusher grades upon that road as I am informed; one against western traffic and one against eastern traffic. One of these is in New Brunswick, it is about 12 mile slong, it is against western traffic, it rises southerly from the Tobique river to the head waters of the Miramichi, the Tate of rise being 1 l-10th per cent or 59 feet in the mile, or in all 708 feet. The other pusher grade to which I allude is in the province of Quebec and is with the western traffic and against the eastern traffic. It occurs in getting down from the Quebec summit to the St. John waters; it is of about the same length as the other and the grade is about the same, namely,1 l-10th per cent. I do not know whether these grades have been adopted, but I am placing this information before the Minister of Railways in order that he may correct me if I am wrong and that he may place an exact statement of the position in that regard before the House and before the country. I observe by reference to the National' Transcontinental Railway Commissioners' Report for 1907, pages 5 and 6, that there is some comparison of cost between the three surveyed lines between Grand Falls and Chatham, and I assume the one which has been adopted is the central pusher grade which is alluded to in that report. Now, if the comparative merits of the Transcontinental Railway and the Intercolonial Railway between Quebec

and Moncton are estimated on the basis which is adopted in the report of the Transcontinental Commissioners for 1907, there are people in this country who have some knowledge of the subject and who are very much of the opinion that the Intercolonial Railway will have the greater advantage of the two roads. What I desire the Minister of Railways to do is to place before parliament during the committee stage on this Bill such full and complete information as to distances, grades, curvatures, and otherwise both on the Intercolonial Railway and on the National Transcontinental Railway between Quebep and Moncton as would enable an expert to make a correct estimate of the cost of haulage over each road. I think that is a fair and reasonable request, and indeed I do not think that I should be obliged to make it, because I would have thought that if the National Transcontinental Railway possesses that abundant merit which the government claim for it in respect to the section between Quebec and Moncton, during the very first days of the present session we should have had exactly such a statement as I now ask to be placed upon the table of the House. And more than that, we should have had expert opinion submitted which would indicate to the people of Canada what advantage they are to receive from the exxpenditure of $30,000,000 of public money upon the line between Quebec and Moncton. I have already asked the Minister of Railways for his estimate as to deterioration and interest on the line between Quebec and Moncton; I have asked for his views as to the local traffic on that line between Quebec and Moncton; I have asked as to the date of the completion of the Quebec bridge.
I now revert to the question which I dwelt upon a moment ago, and that is as to whether or not the government have made any proposal to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company with respect to the operation of the Quebec-Moncton line during the five or six years before the completion of the Quebec bridge. If you look at the statute and contract of 1904 you will find by section 3, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company is entitled to obtain a lease of any portion of the road which may have been complet'd in advance of the whole line. I do not find that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company is bound tc take a lease of any such portion of the road. I find they are entitled to do it; they have an option there as they have under nearly every one of the provisions of this contract. Thus they are not bound to take it, and therefore the Grand Trunk Pacific Company if they see fit can absolutely decline the operation of that road until the Quebec bridge is completed. That is the contract as I Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
understand it. If hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have a different appreciation of the meaning and effect of that contract, and if they will pledge themselves to this House that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company concurs iq any view different from that which I have just now expressed, then of course the question which I am raising goes by the board to a certain extent and has not the importance 1 am now placing upon it. But as I understand it, the Grand Trunk Pacific Company will not be bound to operate that road until the completion of the Quebec bridge, they being only bound to operate the line as a through line from Winnipeg to Moncton. It would appear that they are not bound to operate it with that link left out. In the very last report of the chief engineer of the Transcontinental Railway, Mr. Lumsden says 'The Quebec bridge is an essential link in the line from Winnipeg to Moncton.' Mark the words ' essential link.' Suppose you take one and a half miles or two miles out of this line anywhere between Moncton and Winnipeg; is the Grand Trunk Pacific bound to operate the two ends of the road or are they only bound to operate the line as a whole. Could they not similarly set up the contention, and will they not set it up, that if you take out of that line one and one-tenth miles at Quebec they cannot operate it as a through line from Winnipeg to Moncton, and in that way may there not be five or six years during which time they will not be obliged to take over this line but leave it upon the hands . of the government. Either this is a difficulty or it is not a difficulty; it seems to me to be a difficulty. If it is a difficulty, it is a very serious difficulty which confronts the government of this country. Again I ask, whether or not under the conditions which have been disclosed to the House by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in introducing this measure, the government have been so occupied with the difficulties of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company that they have absolutely forgotten their own difficulties, and have paid not the slightest attention to the point I am now discussing.
There are just one or two other matters upon which I would like to ask for information from the government, and I give them notice now, so that we may be supplied with it at the earliest possible moment after reaching the comjnittee stage. How is it that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway .Company has been, enabled to provide the money for the building of its branch from Port Arthur to its main line without any assistance from the government, and must needs come to the government for assist-

ance upon the prairie section? We all realize that the branch from Port Arthur to the main line of the National Transcontinental Railway is a very important line to the company. We recall the provisions of the contract under which, so far as the disposition of these branch lines is concerned, the result, roughly speaking, is this, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company can keep what they desire, and compel this country to take the rest. I have no idea that they will ever ask the government of this country to take over the branch from Port Arthur to the main line. That is regarded by people who can speak with authority on the subject, as a key to the operation of the whole Transcontinental Railway system, and it seems rather peculiar that the funds should have fallen short so far as the prairie section is concerned, and that the funds should have been so abundant so far as the branch from Port Arthur to the main line is concerned.
Then, I would like a little more definite reply to the question which has already been proposed across the floor of this House, whether or not the government is prepared to state, in connection with this loan, that it will be the last application for assistance to be made to the people of this country by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, or whether we are to expect a succession of applications for assistance, especially when the construction of the mountain section is begun in earnest. I think the government could not have been so remiss in its duty as not to have put that question fairly and frankly to these gentlemen when they came forward with their application. It is to be presumed that there was some answer, and parliament, while engaged in the consideration of this additional assistance to the amount of $10,000,000, is surely entitled to know what that answer was, and whether this is the last as well as the first application, or whether we are to expect a series of applications covering the whole amount of assistance that will be required in the construction of the mountain section.
As I have said, the country has embarked on this project, it has been ratified by the people of this country as well as by parliament in 1904, and I agree that the work must not stop. If this loan is absolutely necessary, it must be made, in order that the work shall not stop; hut in investigating the terms on which that loan shall be made, the interests of the people of this country ought to be considered in respect of the matters which I have brought to the attention of the House, and ought to be conserved and safeguarded to the fullest possible extent.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend who
has just resumed his seat has maintained his reputation very well for giving the government a large order by way of inquiry. We will endeavour to satisfy his appetite in this respect as far as it is at all possible. It seems to be a difficult one to satisfy, as he comes up hungry on every occasion.

Get your menu card
ready.

I thought our menu card was pretty comprehensive on previous occasions. However, the hon. gentleman is entitled to all the information we can possibly get. The hon. gentleman asks if there will be any other request from the Grand Trunk Pacific for aid. For myself I am not prepared to say; I would not like to accept the responsibility of what any person might do in the future. But this much my hon. friend ought to consider. He says that this enterprise must not stop, and that if it be necessary to make this loan of $10,000,000, it must be made. Suppose the Grand Trunk Pacific Company said to the government and to this House to-day, 'This is the last time of asking, as well as the first;' and suppose that in a few years they forgot or ignored that and asked us for further aid, would not my hon. friend be in exactly the same position that he is in to-day? Would he not have to say: 'Well, the work has commenced, we are partners in the work to a large extent, we may not like to do it, and you promised that you would not ask us; but if it be necessary to complete the work, we must do it.' That is practically the situation we might be in. Therefore I would not like to express an opinion one way or the other. The conditions have to be taken as they arise; and while we are in hopes that the Grand Trunk Pacific, the great project in which we are all so much interested, will now go on to completion successfully, it would be more than human, it would be approaching the prophetic attributes of a higher power to say what might be in the mind of a railway man a few years hence. My hon. friend remarked that the branch from Superior junction to Fort William bad not received any government aid. So far as a guarantee is concerned, that is true. I think it has received a subsidy from this House, and to that extent my hon. friend's information would be incorrect.
I was speaking of applications to the government for assistance.
Perhaps I misunderstood my hon. friend's meaning. What he said was that that branch had not received any assistance from the government.
Had not made any application at the present time for assistance.

That is a different matter. Well, we understand the hon. gentleman's meaning now. I want to make it clear to the House, what they understand without an explanation, that few railways of that extent are constructed without coming to the government for aid, and they generally get it.
How much did you grant it?

The usual government subsidy, and they got something from the Ontario government as well. With reference to the pusher grades east of Quebec, the only object of having good gradients, as I understand it, is for the benefit of transportation. If a condition arises in a particular part of a railway where the use of a pusher grade may be adopted without interfering with transportation, and so as to reduce the cost of the railway, probably it would be right to adopt it. But this much must be borne in mind, that through the long summer months a good deal of the shipment of grain from the west will probably take place through Quebec, and the pusher grade interferes with the transportation only of a very heavy load. The ordinary train does not need to have a pusher to take it over the grade, but it is in developing the transportation problem to the extent of hauling a very large train that a pusher grade is used. I may be asked what a pusher grade means. It simply means a grade where a second engine is used to help to push the train over the summit. East of Quebec there is one pusher grade against east bound traffic and a similar grade against west bound traffic. It is immaterial what are the various meanderings of the railway from this point to another point, from the summit to the depth, except so far as it affects the grade. And notwithstanding the very interesting description of the line, read by my hon. friend, and the various heights it has to climb, it resolves itself into the fact that there are two pusher grades, one against eastbound traffic and the other against westbound traffic. The other facts dwelt on by my hon. friend would simply mean it was an expensive line to build to get rid of the grades. The more uneven the country, the more hills there are to cross, the more mountains to climb and the more valleys to get over, if the grade is to be got rid of, the greater the expenditure in the building and it is true that the expense of building a line in the east is considerable. In district A at the Tobique river there is a pusher grade against the eastbound traffic, for 12-65 miles. That saves in the length of the line 17-2 miles and in the cost of construction approximately nearly $2,000,000.
What is the grade there?
I think my hon. friend described it properly.
One and one-tenth?

I think that is right. In district B near the New Brunswick boundary, there is one against the westbound traffic, JO-7 miles long, said to save a distance of about 18 miles, and a saving in expense of over a million dollars.
What would be the total length of the road between Quebec and Moncton provided the pusher grades were eliminated and the grade was what was originally expected?
There might not be any difference in length if they went to the expense of getting over the pusher grade by cuttings or fillings at that particular point.
I understand that the elimination of these two pusher grades would add 35 miles to the length.
If you got rid of the pusher grade by making a circuit, by going around the acclivity and adding to the length, that might happen.
That would make the road six miles longer than the Intercolonial Eailway, would it not?

We may go on figuring out if this should be the case, and if the other is the case, the following will be the result; but I have not admitted my hon. friend's starting point. If you went round another hill or two, you would make the road considerably longer.
Was the grade I mentioned correct?

I think so. The only question is whether to accept the two pusher grades, considering the traffic from Quebec to Moncton, with the saving that would involve, or remove them. The engineer reports that it is better in those instances to have the pusher grades and save the money.
Are there any pusher grades on the Intercolonial Eailway?

There would be if we had the very large trains these are intended to haul, when they have the western traffic of the Grand Trunk Pacific. There are three very steep grades, as my hon. friend has remarked, on the Intercolonial Eailway. There is one at the Bedford grade,
1 -80, at Folleigh, 1 -22, at Metis, 1 -29. These might be called pusher grades.
That is in both directions.
Yes.
How many west and how many east?
I could not tell that at the moment.
Has the minister any actual report from the engineers that they could have avoided those pusher grades in any way except by lengthening the line some 35 miles?
I have not got them at hand.
Has the hon. minister any such report?

That would be a report from Mr. Lumsden, and my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, has the three reports to which the hon. gentleman refers. Now, we come to the Quebec bridge. It is easy enough, under present conditions, to raise all kinds of criticisms as to the effect of the destruction of the Quebec bridge. But this House is supposed to be composed of practical men, who are not following shadows. No doubt, the collapse of the bridge was a great calamity and we have to face the results. There is no escape from the situation by raising all kinds of possible objections and pointing out the result of the calamity. We admit at once that it was a calamity, and the inconvenience it will cause, and the difficulties which have arisen, are not to be minimized. I do not quite agree with my hon. friend, although I will not say, speaking from memory, that hi is altogether wrong, when he says that the Grand Trunk Pacific will not be compelled to operate the eastern section without the Quebec bridge. The question of the Quebec bridge being a link in the railway is indisputable, so far as the operation of the railway is concerned, but it does not follow that it is a part of the railway itself. The bridge was undertaken before the railway project was outlined, and there would have been a Quebec bridge had there never been a transcontinental railway. But for practical purposes, and for the operation of the line, the bridge is an integral part of the railway.
Under the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific, are you obliged to build the Quebec bridge?
I would not put it as strongly as that, but that is the understanding.
Is it in the contract?

Possibly it is. But the Quebec bridge was to be constructed without any Grand Trunk Pacific contract and was undertaken before that railway was thought of. Consequently that does not add to the cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The
Quebec bridge would have been built had there been no contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend may be sure the government has not at all overlooked the difficulties arising on account of the absence of the Quebec bridge. Not only will that bridge be finished as rapidly as possible, but the difficulties which are arising and which will continue to arise, owing to its not being completed as early as was anticipated, are not being overlooked by the government. Coming to the question of the Grand Trunk Pacific, my hon. friend has outlined that project at great length, and he made one statement, which I think is perhaps the keystone of the whole situation. He said that the government or the country io a partner with the railway company in this great project. My hon. friend makes it a greater partner than, I think, he is entitled to make it, when he names its proportions of holdings as nine-tenths, _ or ninety per cent. But that is immaterial; the foundation of the request for the loan and the granting of it by this government is that the Dominion of Canada is a partner with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in the carrying out of this great project. It is our project as well as theirs, and the interests of Canada and the Canadian people are paramount even to the interest of the railway company in the completion of this line.
Now, this leads me to one or two questions that have arisen. My hon. friend will pardon me if I go back for a moment. The question has been discussed in this House, and has been referred to mildly to-day of the necessity of this road. My hon. friend agrees that there was a necessity for the construction of this line. Let me look for a moment at the remarks made by the Prime Minister in 1903 when he was introducing this measure, and see if there is any part of these remarks which should be retracted by the Prime Minister or by any member of the government or of this House on his behalf. He said that a railway was a national as well as a commercial necessity.
' A railway.'

' A railway.' And my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) will remember that by ' a railway ' he meant, not a line from North Bay westward, but a line from the eastern part of Canada to the western part of Canada all the way on Canadian soil. No person will say to-day, looking at it from a national standpoint, that Canada was not justified and is not now justified in pushing this project to completion as rapidly as possible. Our position as a country is something of which we should be proud. Some hon. members, properly, grew eloquent over the defences of Canada, the necessity for being prepared to defend Canada against intruders who would

attempt to molest her trade, or interfere with her freedom and happiness, or drag her from the position she holds in the British empire. Sir, taking it from that standpoint, one of the first things necessary was a line of railway on Canadian soil over which troops could be carried without interference.
We had that already.
Will my hon. friend (Mr. George Taylor) tell me where?
The Intercolonial from the sea-board to Montreal and the Canadian Pacific from Montreal to the Pacific coast.
That is two lines of railway. My hon. friend is partially correct, but very much wrong.
And practically all right.

As I said before, and my hon. friend cannot contradict it, we had not a great line of railway from eastern Canada to western Canada over which Canadian and British troops could be Car-Tied from one ocean to another without passing over foreign soil. This is looking at _ the question from the national standpoint. But, after all, that is only minor, to my mind. From the commercial standpoint it was necessary to have another through line. This House and this country may think I am altogether too optimistic, but I believe when this line is completed it will be taxed to its utmost capacity with the carrying trade of Canada and the carrying trade from the Orient to Europe. I believe that before many years are over we shall have to look for greater transportation facilities in order to accommodate the increasing trade of this great country. Sir, the words of the Prime Minister are not to be taken back, they stand to-day not only true but fortified by the events that have taken place since they were spoken in 1903. Let me point out one or two things showing the necessity for this road from a commercial standpoint, and as showing the prospects for its success as a transcontinental line. The annual output of coal in the west now is about
4.000.	000 tons. A good authority estimates -and I think he is within the' mark-that thirty years hence there will be at least
50.000.	000 tons of coal to be transported in the west. In the valley of the Saskatchewan, there are about 200,000,000 acres of land, and in the valley of the Mackenzie about 55,000,000 acres. Thirty years ago there were no wheat fields in that vicinity, and scarcely a hamlet in the valley of the Saskatchewan or the valley of the Mackenzie. Let hon. members think of the

west as it is to-day and of the west as it was thirty years ago, and then prophesy, if they can, what, a few years hence, this great and growing west will be, if we do our duty and give the people we are bringing in there proper facilities for getting their products to market. These plains produce to-day, it is no extravagant estimate to say, 100,000,000 bushels of grain yearly.
Now, let me point out the bearing of that as showing the great part that Canada is to play, as I believe, in feeding the nations of the world. The world's population, it is estimated, doubles in fifty years, and the present population of the world is
1,700,000,000 people. We may believe that, in the next fifty years, there will be added to the world's population at least 900,000,000 people. But, while the world's population is increasing, man cannot add one acre to the land on the face of the earth. We may discover other wheat fields, w'e may open up territory that is now lying waste and make it productive in years to come, but the fact remains that poor humanity cannot create one acre of land. So, while the consumption and the demand go on increasing, the land for the production of food remains what it is to-day. Now, Sir, to-day half the population of the world never see any flour of wheat. It is estimated that there are fully 100,000,000 white people who never get enough flour to eat. The demand for this flour among these people is continually growing, and there is this demand to be allowed for as the demand arising out of the increase^ of population in this and other countries. To-day, the prospects are, Canada will be the main wheat field of the world. Should there be any pessimism in the outlook in the minds of people who are today and will be in the future the proprietors of those fields which must feed the people of the world? As the west develops and these millions of acres become productive, Canada will be, to a large extent, the world's granary. I point this out to impress on the minds of the neople of Canada that in our conduct of public affairs, in our dealings with just such questions as this, we must ever keep in mind not the present only, but the great future and the development of the mightv heritage Providence has given us. For, with all our criticism of one another, this stands true, that the Canadian people to-day have one of the most productive countries in the world. Should we hesitate? Should we not have courage in carrying out this great undertaking that the people of Canada have twice said should be carried out? We may disagree on details, as men of common sense wiil always disagree. I appeal to western representatives as well as eastern: Should we not approach such questions as

these with the larger outlook of what Canada is to be in the future? I believe that I will live, if I reach the ordinary span of life, to see Canada, and the west particularly, developed to such an extent that we who now look back fifteen or twenty years and think the development has been great, will be astonished at the increase that will have taken place in the next few years.
Sir, we talk about wheat. Fifteen years ago we sold our wheat for 50 cents, to-day wheat is worth $1.20. Some person may say: That is only the result of a panic, or a corner. I believe that wheat will continue to move upward. It may have its reverses through adverse circumstances; owing to the fact that the wheat producing area is limited, and the consumption is ever increasing, millions of bushels more will be required every year. Sir, I believe that the world, and Canada, has seen the last of cheap wheat, that the price will continue to advance, and I believe that in a few years hence we will be discussing wheat from a $1.50 standpoint rather than $1 standpoint. With this end in view, it seems to be our duty to the people whom we induced to come in and develop our country, to allow them to get their products to the markets of the world in the speediest possible way, at the lowest price, and in the best possible condition. But some one will say; 1 Has the bringing of this railway into the Northwest helped any?' I believe that the projected line has already made a marked improvement in the condition of the western people so far as transportation facilities are concerned. I had intended to place on the table of the House a railway map of 1905 and a railway map of 1909, to let hon. gentlemen see just the number of homesteads that have been taken up in that country since the Grand Trunk Pacific project was introduced into this House. But you say: ' The other railways did that.' Certainly. I wanted also to point out the number of branch lines shown on the map, belonging tc other railway companies that were not there when the Grand Trunk Pacific project was first introduced. You ask me what has that to do with the Grand Trunk Pacific? It has this to do, and every practical man knows, every man from the west, and every man who has been in the Railway Committee of this House, will bear me out in saying that the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific was to go through certain portions of the west induced other great companies to extend their branch lines in every possible direction in order to compete with the Grand Trunk Pacific. If the Grand Trunk Pacific never carried a pound of freight from the west to the east or from the east to the west, the launching of that project has been to a
large extent justified by the improved facilities that other lines have given to the people on account of the proposed construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. But you ask me: ' Have not the people come in along tlie line of the Grand Trunk Pacific? ' Let me point out a thing or two in that connection. In a carefully prepared statement of Mr. R. E. Young, superintendent of railway lands for the Department of the Interior, he estimates that 15,389 homesteads have been taken up in a belt of 12 miles on either side of the Grand Trunk Pacific, 15,389 homesteads on a strip of land 24 miles wide, 12 on either side of the railway, or on a belt of land 8 miles less on each side than were exempted from taxation under the old contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Since how long?

Since the projection of the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend should know that people go ahead of the line, when they once discover in what direction it will run. As a direct result of the Grand Trunk Pacific, to say nothing of the branch lines, to say nothing of the general influx that has been taking place in other parts of that country, since the projection of this line, on 12 miles on each side of the railway 15,389 homesteads have been taken up, equal to 2,461,928 acres. If I had time to go into the details, I might figure out what the cultivation of 2,461,928 acres means to the people of the west, if no more were taken up.
You might also figure out how large a porportion of these homesteads are within a nearer distance of another parallel line of railway.

My hon. friend will remember that this parallel line of railway was there before, but the people were not; and he will remember the fact that they went there because they are 'to have the Grand Trunk Pacific competition, which they otherwise would not have had. Now, Sir, we have also prepared a statement of the population, and I trust the House will not weary with me if I give it, because it has a bearing on the advisability of seeing that this project is put through with all necessary speed. In 1906, Manitoba had 365,688; in 1908, 462,569. In 1906, Saskatchewan had 257,763; in 1908, 335,721. In 1906, Alberta had 185,413; in 1908, 265,820. This shows an increase of over 25 per cent. Sir, with the population of the west increasing so ranidly, this government could not hesitate, if the proposition of the Grand Trunk Pacific were less favourable than it is, and the people of this country would not allow us to hesitate, in seeing to it that nothing is left undone to give proper

facilities to this ever increasing population.
Now, I think I have shown fairly well that the words of my right hon. friend, the leader of the government, in introducing this project into the House have been more than justified by the influx of people into the west. A great deal has been said about the cost of the line, and that seems to be the chief complaint made against this project. We even find our friends from the west complaining that we are building lines that are too poorly constructed, that will not carry the traffic they have, the bridges of which are not strong enough, the rails of which are not heavy enough, the ballast of which is not well enough placed, the curvature and grades of which are not of the proper kind. Sir, that is not the criticism that we hear of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The only criticism we hear of this Grand Trunk Pacific line from railway men is that we are building it of too high a standard, that it would be better to build it of a lower standard and improve it as the years went by. That is one method of building railways, but I think I will be able to show that that would be poor economy. I think the best economy is to build a line that will be able to carry its full freight, at the proper price, the first day a train is run over it, rather than to carry small trains and be obliged to improve the road year after year, robbing it of its income, as well as its capital expenditure, and getting, perhaps, after 20 years, as good a road as we now mean to make it on the first day it is run. Now the question of cost comes in.
I need not again traverse in detail the statement made time and again as to the increased cost of material and wages, the higher standard of the road and the benefits to be derived. I know my hon. friend will say: Yes, the road is of a very high standard, but the people of Canada were told in 1903 that it was to be of the standard of the line of the Grand Trunk Railway between Montreal and Toronto. Sir, the standard of the Transcontinental line is a higher standard than the standard of the Grand Trunk Railway between Montreal and Toronto. The grades are less and in every respect the standard is as high and in some respects higher than that of the Grand Trunk between those two cities at the time this contract was made. Some people will say: 'Yes, but they have laid steel rails of 100 pounds to the yard and double tracked the line between Toronto and Montreal.' But there were no steel rails of 100 pounds to the yard at the time the contract was made and the specification in the contract as to the standard referred to conditions then existing. Any Mr. GRAHAM.
man who has travelled from Montreal to Toronto on the Grand Trunk line knows that it is one of the best lines on the continent, and will agree that this is a very high standard, but as far as grades are concerned, it is not as high as the Transcontinental line between Moncton and Winnipeg or even Moncton and the eastern side of the Rocky mountains.

I would not answer the hon. gentleman in the way he suggests, because I have quoted already the language of the Minister of Finance in 1903 or 1904 when he said he was estimating on a four-tenth per cent grade. He will find that language at page 3687 of this year's ' Hansard.'
The contract, I think, will bear out my statement that the standard was to be the standard of the Grand Trunk Railway between Montreal and Toronto.
That is quite so, but I was -speaking of the estimates.

A good deal has been said about the estimates. Mr. Schreiber's estimate was made in 1903 before the contract was made. Whatever difference of opinion there may be, there is no doubt that Mr. Schreiber had not in his mind the high standard which the country has exacted in making the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific, but rather had in mind a road like the Intercolonial Railway with its gradients and lighter rail, of 65 pounds instead of 80 pounds. But there are other factors which tend to increase the cost. Labourers' wages, which were $1.25 to $1.50 per day at that time have increased to $2.25. Ties, which were 25 cents and 28 cents, have increased to 50 and 60 cents. Timber and lumber for use in culverts, trestles, &c., has increased from 30 and 32 cents to 38 cents and 40 cents. Steel rails have increased in price from $25 or $28 a ton in 1903 to $35 or $36 in 1908 and a duty has been added since then of some $7 per ton. Then the rails used, instead of being 65 pounds are 80 pounds to the yard, a difierence of 23 tons to the mile. These facts account for a portion at least of the increase in the cost of the road.
I do not wish to go further with this comparison but to simply point out that the cost of all kinds of material and labour has increased and that the road is of a higher standard than was anticipated by Mr. Schreiber. Further than that, I make the statement without any fear of contradiction that for a transcontinental line or one approaching a transcontinental line the standard of the Grand Trunk Pacific is the highest on the continent of America. Of the mountain section about 100 miles is under construction and a good deal of dif-

ference of opinion exists as to its cost.
I have an opinion by a gentleman who I think has a fairly good knowledge of the conditions, that he believes that the mountain section, with the exception of one or two points, will not average a higher cost than the cost of the Lake Superior pertion of the eastern section. He believes the construction is not any heavier in the greater part of the mountain section than it is in portions of the eastern section being built by the government. The suggestion that it would cost $100,000 per mile is altogether out of reason.
The minister must see that in order to understand that, we must have an idea as to what the eastern section would cost.

My hon. friend will find that information in returns I have brought down as to the different sections. I have the contract price according to sections.
But, speaking of the advanced cost,_ is this the only line, is this the only project in which the cost has greatly exceeded the estimate? I need not refer to large undertakings, I need only refer any hon. gentleman who has built a house to his own experience. If he looks up his accounts he will find that the house has cost him a good deal more than he estimated. I wish to make one other comparison. We have heard the Panama canal quoted as a sample of what could be done and the economies that could be effected by the appointment of a good commission. In speaking of the cost of building the Transcontinental Railway by a commission, the question of the personnel of such a commission would naturally come under review. I wish to point out that in the criticisms of the Transcontinental Commission I have not yet found anything which would lead me to believe that this commission have not performed and are not performing their work in an able and conscientious manner. When the American government undertook the construction of the Panama canal, they selected certain commissioners who were said to be very efficient. But these commissioners remained only a short time, they were not allowed to complete the canal, and were replaced by other men. The men who replaced them were again replaced by other men so that a comparison of the selection of commissions on the Panama canal and on the Transcontiental Railway does not reflect discredit on the Transcontinental Commission. The commission now entrusted with the construction of the Panama canal is composed of military engineers on the staff of the United States War Department, with the addition of one or two other men, and it is now directly under government control. Being members of the military staff the present Panama 162
Canal Commission are not so open to criticism and fault-finding and tale-bearing, if I might use that expression, they are under more thorough discipline both as to work and talk than they otherwise would be.
As to the cost of the Panama canal, may I point out that with all the care that was exercised by the first commission, the second commission and lastly the government commission, the original estimate will be greatly exceeded. The first estimate for the Panama canal was $140,000,000. The sum did not include the purchase price of $50,000,000 nor the cost of sanitation and civil government of the canal zone, $27,000,-
000.	By putting all this in-which for arugment sake might be compared if omitted to omitting the Quebec bridge from the Canadian project-by putting all this in we have $217,000,000. But the board of experts with Mr. Taft reported in February, 1909, that the cost would be not $217,000,000, but $360,000,000, or an increase of $143,000,000. And Colonel Boutelle, chief engineer, before the House committee on appropriations placed the estimate not at $360,000,000 but at $375,000,000, and if we take the interest during construction as is taken in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific, we will find that the Panama canal project which has been cited as an example, of economy and good management was at first estimated to cost $217,000,000, and that the present estimate when it is not merely completed, is $400,000,000 or nearly twice as much as the original estimate. I will cite some other instances to show to the country that all this talk about increased cost over the estimate is not peculiar to the National Transcontinental Railway alone but is common to every project private or public in this or any other country. The New York Erie barge canal was estimated in 1899 to cost $61,536,788, but two years afterwards the board of experts estimated the cost at $94,000,000, a difference of $32,764,484 or an increase between 1899 and 1901 of something over 50 per cent. But in 1903, two years later again, the state engineer revised that estimate and raised it from $94,000,000 to $100,562,993, and in chapter 147 of the laws of New York you will find an act authorizing them to borrow $100,000,000 for this canal which originally was estimated to cost $61,000,000. And, if we include the interest as is done in the case of the National Transcontinental Railway it is safe to say that the Erie barge canal which was estimated to cost $61,000,000 will exactly cost $125,000,000, or more than 100 per cent extra.
You must estimate the interest in both cases.
That should be a warning against your predictions.
It should be a warning against any hon. gentleman citing the Panama canal as an example.
Surely the Minister of Railways does not pretend to say that the engineering work on the Transcontinental Railway can be compared in difficulty with the engineering work on the Panama canal.

The hon. gentleman will understand that the engineers of the Panama canal were engaged as experts to give the people of the country an estimate of what it would cost including all the engineering difficulties. Let me point out further that taking the details day in and day out, the difficulty of estimating a line through the Rock mountains and from one end of Canada to the other is approximately as great as estimating the cost of the Panama canal, and I think you will find some competent engineers who will say it is more difficult to estimate the cost of the Transcontinental Railway. Now, Sir, I want to make this statement which may be considered a strong statement, and I w ant it to be considered strong; I say that not only will we have the highest standard transcontinental line on this continent, but we will have a line that will cost no more than any line similarly situated under like circumstances which has been built anywhere during the last 15 years. Let me cite as an example the cost of one or two other lines of railway. The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Company are building a line from Evarts, South Dakota, to Seattle, Washington, 1,500 miles long. They started that line about the same time as the Transcontinental Railway and the maximum grade is 52 feet to the mile as compared with 21 feet on the National Transcontinental Railway. It is estimated that road will cost over $60,000 per mile on the authority of the 'Financial Chronicle,' and a large portion of that road is through territory, I am informed by engineers, comparatively speaking on a par with the prairie section of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
What will their prairie section cost?
If I were to make the statement as strong as my informant makes it, I would say that it is nearly all prairie section, but I would not like to say that.
Surely it has to pass through the Rocky mountains to reach Seattle.
It can't get there any other way.
It is certainly not all prairie.
I certainly admit that it will have to run through the Rocky mountains.
Between what points did you say the line ran?

From Evarts, South
Dakota, to Seattle.
You will not find much prairie section there.

My statement is on the authority of engineers who say they have been over that territory. At all events the cost of that road is $60,000 per mile as given by the ' Financial Chronicle ' which is considered to be an absolute authority.
Do not the Rocky mountains intervene between these two points?

Most assuredly they do. Nature has not removed the mountains, and I do not attempt to make a prairie section over the mountain portion. The Western Pacific is building a line from Salt Lake City, Utah, to San Francisco, California, 929 miles, and although the maximum grade is 52 feet to the mile as against our 21 feet, that road will cost over $70,000 per mile.
All in the mountains.
Not all in the mountains.
With a cut-off across Salt lake.
Approximately speaking my hon. friend may say that a large portion of that line is in the Rocky mountains but it is not all in the mountains.
What about the cut-off?
