INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
1.	In what amount, if any, is the Grand Trunk Railway Company indebted to the Dominion of Canada?
2.	How much is owing for principal and interest, respectively, upon the said indebtedness ?
3.	How many years' interest is due?
4.	On what date was interest last paid?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
This deals with a very old and complicated account. It might be more convenient to put it as a motion for return, but as I thought the hon. gentleman (Mr. George Taylor) might regard it as having a bearing on proposals of this ssesion, I have brought down the answer:
1, 2, 3 and 4. In the year 1862, five years prior to confederation, a reorganization of the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada was . fleeted under chapter 56 of the Statutes of Canada of that year.
Provincial debentures of the provinces of Canada to the amount of $15,142,633.34 had been issued, prior to the passing of this Act, in aid of the company. These debentures carried interest at the rate of six per cent per annum.
By section 19, of the chapter referred to, the province of Canada consented to allow its claim for interest due and accruing in respect of these debentures to be postponed to the payment of certain charges which were made prior by the statute. The section provided that after the payment of the working expenses of the railway the balance of earnings was to be appropriated and applied in payment:-(a) of interest on

equipment mortgage bonds; (b) of interest on first preferential bonds and tbe dividend due on first preference stock; (c) of interest due on second preferential bonds and the dividend due on second preference stock; (d) cf dividend due on third preference stock; ;e) of dividend due on fourth preference siock; (f) of dividend of 3 per cent per annum for ten years on the ordinary stock of [DOT]tne company and thereafter at the rate of i per cent per annum; (g) of further dividend on one per cent per annum on the third preference stock; (h) of further dividend of one per cent per annum on the fourth preference stock; (all the above were given priority over the government claim for interest) ; and then: (i) in payment of the interest for the time being due and accruing, subsequent to the 1st January, 18(52, on the provincial debentures issued in aid of the company, before the passing of the Act, at the rate of 6 per cent per annum.
The interest on the provincial debentures referred to amounted, at the time of confederation, to $10,457,458.01. Amounts, represented by these province of Canada debentures, $15,142,633.34 and this interest of $10,457,458.01 were, at confederation, taken over by the Dominion from the province of Canada, and have since then carried in the balance sheet without change under the heading ' Railway Accounts/ but these amounts have not been included in the statement of assets of the Dominion.
As the net earnings of the company never met all the prior charges, as provided by the Act, no part of this interest has ever been payable.
There was also carried in the province of Canada accounts and taken over at confederation a special interest claim of $7,302.18, which has been continued in the balance sheet. This special interest claim arose from an adjusted balance of various accounts made between the province of Canada and the C- rand Trunk Railway Company which balance was confirmed by an order in council cf the 18th October, 1866.
Besides the above, the province of Canada was, at the time of confederation, the holder of fourth preference stock of the company, (converted, by section 11, chapter 18, Act of 1873, into third preference stock), of the par \alue of $121,739.65. Coming now to the loan, which is the subject of the Bill 1. if ore vhe (louse, the whole question is this-not what has the Transcontinental Commission done between Moncton and Winnipeg, not what has the Mr. GRAHAM.
government done, not whether the Quebec bridge has fallen down, not whether the gradients of the eastern section of the Grand Trunk Pacific are pusher grades or four-tenths of one per cent or six-tenths of one per cent, not whether the ferry will be run at Quebec, not whether there will be local traffic on the Transcontinental east of Quebec. The question before the House and the country is: Under the conditions existing, is it in the interest of the people of Canada to grant a loan of $10,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company? I say most unhesitatingly it is. My bon. friend says we ought to ask them for $10,000,000 of preference bonds. I say we are not presenting the Grand Trunk Pacific Company with anything. We are allowing them to issue bonds, which we will take as security, guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, and we will hold those bonds, as the Minister of Finance has remarked, merely as security for the payment of this loan; and if on the issue of these bonds they were put on the market and sold, all the liability the government has and all the risk it is taking is the difference between what they would sell at and their par value. We are not giving the company a loan without security; we are not taking security on a piece of railway either; but we are taking security which is guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, which, if it is getting so much as hon. gentlemen say, if it is being placed in such a position of affluence and wealth as they represent, is gilt edge securitv for this loan. It should be remembered too that the stock which my hon. friend proposes as security would only be valuable after the bonds held by the government are provided for. The government, as I have said, is a partner in this great undertaking, and no matter what the conditions might be, the Dominion of Canada could not allow the Grand Trunk Pacific project to fail. It has undertaken it, and what Canada has undertaken Canada is prepared to carry out, whether this government or hon. gentlemen opposite are in power. As they deemed it wise when in power to come to the aid of the Canadian Pacific Railway, although they had aided it bountifully in the first place, so I believe they will not take the position that it would be wise on the part of the Dominion of Canada at the present moment to refuse to grant the request of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, for in granting that request we are making secure the carrying out of a project in which the hon. leader of the opposition himself said we have nine-tenths interest while they have one-tenth.

My hon. friend forgets the principle upon which aid has been

given to railways in the Dominion of Canada. Did we get any stock in the Canadian Pacific Railway?

speechtext: We were not partners.

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes, we are partners, speaking broadly. Why was the Canadian Pacific Railway aided if it was not in the interest of the people?

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Who said anything about interest of the people? My hon. friend must not put in my lips words which I did not utter. I said not a word about interest of the people. I said we were not partners with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the country was not a partner with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in the benefits it was receiving from the railway, then the people of Canada gave the Canadian Pacific Railway Company benefits for which it got no return.

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does the minister believe that?

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not believe it, but my hon. friend tries to get around it by a play on words. He has great ability, I know, in the use of language; but I do not propose to let him get away with a play on words. The people of Canada are partners in every railway that helps the development of the country; if they are not, they have no right to aid railways. Do we aid railways for the amount of stock we are going to get in them? No. We give them money, municipalities give them bonuses, provincial governments give them subsidies-and sometimes land grants, as in Ontario during the last few weeks-provincial governments guarantee their bonds, Dominion governments guarantee their bonds. This government gave the Canadian Pacific Railway 25,000,000 acres of land, a large stretch of line already constructed and $25,000,000 of money; and if that does not make the country a partner with the company, then nothing at all can make a partnership so far as the development of Canada is concerned. When i speak of a partnership, I do not mean a partnership which provides that the government must get stock for stock and share for share, but a partnershio in this Tespect, that our interests run parallel with those of the railways in the development of the country, and in order to get that development and to benefit ourselves we grant aid in different ways to the construction of railways, and thus in the broad sense become partners with them, are responsible to the people of Canada and the British empire for the development of this part of the empire. We give a certain amount of aid.

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend is one of them. We are the people of Canada.

The government come down with a proposal to give $10,000,000 to assist the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to finish the prairie section which they contracted with this government in 1904 to build. In order to understand the matter fully, it would be necessary to consider the whole position in relation to the railway. It was only a few short years ago that the government came to this House with a proposal to build a transcontinental railway from the Atlantic to the Pacific with modern grades, through our own territory. They told us what the road would cost. I stated at the time that the cost would be largely in excess of the government's estimate. My friend the leafier of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) stated-and so did the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding)- that the total cost to the country would be $13,000,000 or less. We laughed at the idea. We have now an acknowledgment that this road from Moncton to Winnipeg will cost in the neighbourhood of $180,000,000, by the time you get not only the road but the Quebec bridge and terminals required for operation of the railway all paid for. A very pertinent question was put by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) as to the gradients on the road between Levis and Moncton, and as to the need for building this road. I remember stating, when the question was before the House, that a better line could not be found between Moncton and Levis than that over which the Intercolonial was built. The line they propose to take had been surveyed by the Intercolonial engineers, but it was not accepted. We find now that they have got a line barely 29 miles shorter than the Intercolonial between Levis and Moncton. And the gradients are the same, because there are two pusher grades, one of 1 and one of l-10th, on this new line, and there are only three on the Intercolonial. And the cost of this new line is over $30,000,000. If one-tenth of the money had been expended in bettering the grades on the Intercolonial, we should have had a better line than either and the country would have saved $27,000,000. But what is $27,000,000 to these gentlemen? The object of this road from Moncton to Winnipeg, they say, is to bring the western grain to our maritime province ports. But is there any one in this country foolish enough to believe that a single bushel of grain-well, perhaps, a few bushels, but any considerable proportion of the crop-will come from Winnipeg to St. John or Halifax over the Grand

Trunk Pacific Railway? However, we are in for it. The Minister of Railways boldly says that we are partners in the road that is now under construction. And, after all, we have no interest in the road. Some time ago when the Bill came before the House, the government assured us that the prairie section would not cost over $17,000 a mile, and the maximum amount to be paid was $13,000 per mile, leaving us to believe that it would cost less than that. Now the estimate is in the neighbourhood of $33,000 per mile, or more than double the original estimate. Engineers make mistakes, the Minister of Finance says, the price of labour has gone up, there has been a duty on steel rails. Every one who knows the condition of the country now and the condition in 1904, is aware that there is no jurisdiction for the statement of the Minister of Finance that the increased expenditure is_ due to an increase in the cost of material. He could easily find out what railroads cost on the prairie, he has only to write to the directors of the Northern Railway. He quoted the report of Sir Thomas Shaughnessy to his directorate as to the cost of that Toad north of Toronto. He could just as easily have ascertained what the cost of the prairie section was likely to be, which is similar. The Grand Trunk Pacific are building a road from Winnipeg to Edmonton, a road of similar character to this, that will not cost in excess of $25,000 per mile. Yet we are called upon to pay $32,000 per mile. What is the position? We were to have a first security on the prairie and on mountain sections for the money advanced, but by the legislation of last year we were piaced pari passu with parties who had mortgages second to ours on these two sections. We have now no preferential claim, we cannot take over that road and work it by a receiver or in any other way except in the interest of the other bondholders who rank pari passu with us, and after putting the bondholders of the road m that position we are to advance them $10,000,000. The Minister of Railways says: . Oh look at the glorious prospect in the Northwest, 200,000,000 acres of land to be opened up on the Saskatchewan river and I do not |
know how many more on the Mackenzie river; think, he says, of the prospect of that immense country that empire that will yet furnish the world with food stuffs within a time which we may expect to see. You would think that all these things would strike investors in an undertaking of this kind and render it more easy for the railway company to raise money. The strongest possible reason which the government could urge for not advancing $10,000,000 to this railway company is that they are building a road through a magnificent section of the country. We pay eight-tenths of the cost of the road and interest for a number of years upon it. Why is it not possible, with such grand prospects, before them for the company to raise the $10,000,000? One.would think that the government in advancing this money would take all the securities which the company have to offer. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) asks the government why they do not get possession of the stock of the company. That might not be of very great benefit after all but we have a right to it. We have also a right to a claim or lien such as the Grand Trunk Railway possesses upon that road from Port Arthur to Winnipeg, which is the key to the situation, but that is left out of our security altogether, we have no claim upon it. What would a road leading from Winnipeg or Edmonton down to this section of the country be without a branch to Lake Superior? It would be a useless undertaking. The hon. gentleman pictures to himself immense trains of grain crossing over this Grand Trunk Pacific from the fertile prairies to the maritime provinces. Does he or any man in this section of the country think that any large quantity of grain will pass the head of Lake Superior by rail? The grain will naturally seek the channel of cheapest transportation, and that is the water route to the sea-coast. The construction of the road to Quebec and Moncton does not promise to be profitable. I hope sincerely that the development in that section of the country from the discovery of minerals, timber and good lands may be such that it will have a bright future, but I do not believe in the manner in which that road is being constructed. The same system of construction should be adopted as is pursued in the case of other roads built through sections of the country which do not at the time of construction furnish sufficient products to afford a profitable traffic. The road should be built as the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, and all other roads in the United States and then as the country developed and traffic increased the road should be improved. But this gentleman says that all these immense crops from the Northwest can be transported to the maritime provinces on a four-

tenths per cent grade from the mountains to the' Atlantic, and that this through traffic will pay the cost of the road. But the cost of the road is not simply the interest we have to pay; we have to consider the danger that the road may be thrown on our hands in the future, especially that portion of it from Winnipeg to Moncton so that we will_ lose not only the interest on its construction but also the immense sum annually which our experience in the government operation of railroads leads us to expect will be lost in its operation.
I observe that the Grand Trunk say they want only $9,400,000 but the chief engineer of our railways says that $10,000,000 and some odd thousands will be required to finish it. That is a difference of only about a million dollars. This money apparently is needed to recoup the bankers of the Grand Trunk Railway Company for money which they advanced to the Grand Trunk for the building of this road. I do not think we are called upon to complete the section of the road with the amount of money and bonds remaining unsold. According to the statement of the Grand Trunk people themselves it will require about $2,000,000 to finish the western section. There will shortly be available $1,-
400,000	of rolling stock and construction rolling stock which can be transferred over from the prairie section to the mountain section as $1,000,000 worth has already been transferred, and the prairie section will get credit for that so that we will have at the most $1,000,000 to provide for. This then is a loan not to assist the Grand Trunk Pacific to construct their road but to recoup the Grand Trunk Railway for money advanced by them to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in a manner which the Finance Minister says he does not quite understand, they borrowed the money from some bank in order to put it into the undertaking. I shall reserve further criticism until we reach the committee stage and have more detailed information.

speechtext: I do not wish to take up the time of the House, but I wish to enter my dissent against this transaction as strongly as I possibly can. Those who were in the House will recall that when the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme was first brought to the notice of the House and of the public there was a universal agreement among the members that further railway accommodation across the continent was necessary. Attempts have been made to show that the Conservative opposition of the day were opposed to the building of a national transcontinental railway, but every one who has followed the debates knows that we were agreed as to the necessity of another transcontinental line, although we absolutely differed from the government as to the method of supplying it.

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Under ordinary circumstances it is possible that I for my part would approve of this loan, but under the circumstances in which it presents itself to us I must emphatically enter my dissent. I remember declaring in this House that the scheme submitted by the government was not the scheme suggested by the Grand Trunk Railway Company at all, and the Minister of Finance will remember that at the end of the lengthy debate on the National Transcontinental Railway Bill he was obliged to produce before the House a document setting forth what the Grand Trunk Company had proposed. The Grand Trunk Railway had a net work of railways in Ontario and Quebec with extensions into the United States, but it lacked an entry into the rich territory of the Northwest, and it proposed to extend to the Pacific ocean so as to provide western connections for its eastern system. Had the plans submitted by the Grand Trunk originally been carried out it would have cost us comparatively little money, and to-day we would easily be able to meet the demands of the company, instead of having to provide for the fearful expenditure which now faces us. Instead of adopting the proposal of the Grand Trunk the government decided to construct this serpentine, circuitous, extraordinary railroad which is going to saddle the country with an expenditure of over $150,000,000. It was plain to everybody at the time, that the project of the government could not be carried out except at enormous expense. The Prime Minister who has a great many admirable qualities but who is neither a railroad builder nor a financier, told us with pathos that the project would cost us $13,000,000 and he added with a wave of the hand that it was only the surplus of one year, and this government glories in its surpluses.

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: However it gets them.

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
However it gets them, and no matter what may be the opinion of political economists as to the surpluses. We on this side argued that the road would cost us over $100,000,000, and the Minister of Railways has to admit that it must cost us $113,000,000. I think we are fairly safe in saying now that the country will have spent over $160,000,000 on the National Transcontinental Railway by the time we have it completed. It was stated when the project was launched in this parliament that this railway would develop the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec, and during the elections which followed, the Conservatives were attacked in Quebec because we had denounced this absurd scheme and declared that it threatened to ruin the country. We were told that we were antagonistic to this railway because we had a hatred of the province

of Quebec and were opposed to its development. I remember arguing at the time in the House that the two older provinces of Ontario and Quebec were certainly entitled to railway development, and that if we had the money there were other expenditures that might better be made. I said that what we required in my native province was the development of colonization lines which beginning at the valley of the St. Lawrence would extend north and south into these portions of the province which had no railway. I said that in Quebec we required colonization roads which would open up that province and bring the traffic down to the St. Lawrence which is the natural outlet for our trade. I presented motions to that effect but these motions were voted down. Can anything more ridiculous be imagined than the construction of a rival road to the Intercolonial Railway between Quebec and Moncton? Is there a man in Canada outside of this House, who does not point out at once this radical objection which vitiates this part of the scheme? We all know that in the territory between Quebec and Moncton there are companies incorporated to build railways which if they were properly assisted would infinitely better develop that district of the province of Quebec than does that section of the Transcontinental Railway. But, instead of encouraging by money grants and otherwise the construction of these railways which would be feeders to the Intercolonial Railway, we are building a rival road, 29 miles shorter between Quebec and Moncton and paralleling for a considerable distance the present government owned road. Well, we prophesied in 1903 that this scheme would not stand, and we are prophesying to-day that the proposal now before us is but the first of a series which will impose further obligations upon the country. The fact will remain that when this line is finally built the country will have paid for it but will not own it, a thing which is contrary to the principles I hold in reference to such public utilities. In the following year, I think,- 1 am speaking from memory-the National Transcontinental was placed by an enactment of this legislature in this situation. We are told that we are going to lease it, that we have a good tenant for the road, and therefore that although we are expending these hundreds of millions upon its construction, we are sure to recover the interest out of the rental which the road will yield. Where is our tenant, and what certainty have we that we shall ever collect one dollar of that rental, under the second step which we made in the evolution of this very unfortunate scheme which we have not seen the end of by any means.
As I understand it, we are in this position. The Grand Trunk Company will become the user of that road when we shall have expended 180 millions upon it. If the Grand Trunk, under its exploitation, cannot pay the rental, what becomes of our tenant? He is absolved from any obligation to pay the rent to this extent, that if the Grand Trunk Railway cannot pay it, the only recourse the country has under that statutory enactment is to place the whole concern in the hands of a receiver, who will distribute what money he can make out of it in certain indicated ways.
When I hear that this railroad is going to become a great grain-carrying road to our sea-board, I entertain very serious doubts. In the first place, as between rail carriage and water carriage, there never will be any competition possible, because water carriage will always be cheaper, and in winter I cannot conjure up, whatever effort of imagination I may make, the idea that any considerable portion of the grain of the west is going to be carried over that road to the Atlantic. There is nothing to prevent the Grand Trunk from realizing the idea which it had in the very inception of this enterprise, and which I regret very much was not carried out, after traversing the plains of the west, and coming into Ontario, to connect with its own system; and does anybody think that with the branch lines 'that will tap the Transcontinental, in the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec, the Grand Trunk will bring any grain it may carry, not to its own network of railways and over its usual route, but through this vast wilderness of the north and down to the lower provinces? I do not believe it. Neither will the Canadian Northern nor the Canadian Pacific. Their interests are all to bring the grain to their own systems of railway and their own ports, and they will do it; and this will never be a graincarrying road. Under these circumstances, it is proper for one who at that time foresaw what is happening to-day, to recall the attitude taken at the time, and to base on that attitude a protest against this loan. Because in an enterprise of this magnitude, where there has been such an entire difference as to the method of carrying it out-I say the method advisedly, because our hon. friends opposite are always asserting that we are against the completion of new and improved means of communication between the east and the west-I say it is proper for one who was opposed to that method at that time, to say that he does not believe in this loan. This loan is a consequence of what was done then, and I as one who -was opposed to the scheme at that time, am opposed to the consequences of that scheme. Now, the loan itself does not commend itself to me on account of the circumstances and

conditions that surround it. If we now have to break up the contract that was made solemnly a few years ago, why are we not given the very best conditions? My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, when he first presented this project, told us that he placed very small reliance upon the mortgage security. I entirely concur in that view. I have very little reliance on a fourth mortgage. I would place more, as my hon. friend did at the time he made the announcement, upon the hope that the road will pay, and that our personal recourse against the road will become good. But can we not get anything better? Here is a company that has in its treasury $20,000,000 of common stock. Who owns it? The shareholders of this company. The stock is_ held in trust by three of them, and it is better than a fourth mortgage. Everybody admits that. No man will rise in this House to deny it. Why can that not be given to us as a security, as it could if the company wished it? Why are we not given preference stock? There is no possible difficulty about that stock, as it is in the company's treasury. Then, there is a company composed, I think, of men who are interested in this enterprise, and formed for the purpose of purchasing town sites along the line of this railway, which of course will become daily more valuable as the line is constructed. That would be good security for our loan. That company is going to enrich these fortunate men. They .are going to become millionaires by the construction of this railway and by the re-sale of these town sites along the line of a road which, as the hon. leader of the opposition has said, we are financing almost entirely with our own money. There are three kinds of securities that are infinitely better than the one mentioned in this Bill.
Aj.e we now getting the very best security since we are asked to depart from the terms of the original contract. That is the second reason why I wish to enter my dissent to this transaction. At present we have urgently needed public works, the construction of which should not be delayed. We have to provide increased accommodations for our friends in the west. That was the original plan of Mr. Hays when he came here to ask government assistance in order to place the vast net work of the Grand Trunk Railway system in contact with that rich region. We have to increase our canal facilities. Since we have thrown into the waste paper basket the report of the Transportation Commission, with all its practical suggestions, our American neighbours have awakened to the necessity of increasing their facilities for water transport; and while we are neglecting our plain duty they are building and deepening canals to tap our trade. Not only was the report of that commission unanimous in recommending the immediate construction of the Mr. MONK.

Instead we have taken upon our shoulders this National Transcontinental Railway, which must for many - years to come absorb all our re-1 sources. That was the scheme we condemned at the time and I condemn it now. Experience has justified what we said at the time, and I wish to enter my protest against this transaction under the circumstances. *

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I am bound, like my chieftain for the province of Quebec, to protest against the proposition which is now laid down before us. I was against that project of railway from the very beginning, and in 1904 I have fought indeed against that project of railway because it was untimely and not enough elaborate.
I consider to-day that we must accept the accomplished fact, that we are too much involved, that we cannot turn back and that we cannot frustrate the endeavours made nor the expenditure incurred. But in another point of view, it does not follow that we are bound to approve of every thing which has been made.
The Conservative party has never been against the construction of railways; it has been on the contrary, always identified with all these undertakings in our country. It has built the Canadian Pacific Railway -the first transcontinental-and that line was built, I can say it, in spite of the persisting hostilities of the Liberal party as a whole.

I am speaking for myself but I am satisfied that the Conservative party, as a party, will not try to kill that enterprise and will not fall into the exaggerations of the Liberal party from 1880 to 1884.
However the conservative party is entitled to see through this matter, and as a matter of fact we are only beginning to get an insight into it.
When we are told that the people have approved in 1904, and ratified in 1908 this undertaking on the part of the government I fail to see on what grounds such a statement is made. In 1904, the people endorsed the building of a railway which, according to the right hon. gentleman himself was to cost about thirteen millions or thereabouts. They endorsed the building of a railway, which according to the Minister of Finance-a man who should have been well posted on the matter-was to cost $11,512,325.
What do we see now? That same undertaking is to cost two or three hundred millions, at any rate over two hundred millions; which goes to show that the people had not been supplied with sufficient information in 1904. I find some further evidence on that point in the columns of the Witness, a paper generally well informed and whose loyalty to the liberal party is well known. The quotation is -is follows:
The following is a brief summary of the principal facts to date; Expended on National Transcontinental Railway from Moncton to Winnipeg, $50,000,000; required to complete it, $66,000,000; required to build prairiesec-tion of Grank Trunk Pacific, $32,000,000; required to build mountain section of Grand Trunk Pacific, $68,000,000; total probable cost from coast to coast, $250,000,000; original estimated cost, $100,000,000; length of line east of Winnipeg, 1,752 miles; under construction, out of 3,556 miles, 2,000 miles. It will be seen from these figures that very much remains to be done, and that the original figures are very far astray indeed. If there were any chance of similar disparity between the estimated cost of building the Georgian Bay canal and the actual cost, the country would be likelv to hesitate very long indeed before embarking on that enterprise.

speechtext: What about the remarks that your honourable chief (Mr. Borden) made a few days ago about the construction of the Georgian Bay canal?

subtopic: INDEBTEDNESS OF GRAND TRUNK RAIL- WAT TO DOMINION GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Allow me to get to the end of this quotation.
It is interesting in this connection to note that the Canadian Pacific Railway, with over twelve thousand miles of railway, with big fleets on two oceans and the great lakes, with a chain of big hotels across the continent, enormous workshops and a rolling stock unsurpassed in the world for size and quality,
only has an issued capital stock of $150,000,000, preference stock $48,800,000, debenture stock $115,650,000, and mortgage bonds of $39,620,000, or a total indebtedness of about $350,000.-
000.
Compare this with the Grand Trunk Pacific's 3,556 miles and its debt of $250,000,000, and the conclusion will soon be reached that if all this money were only honestly expended there is every reason why the Grand Trunk Pacific should be the 'finest and most substantial' railway on the continent. The Canadian Pacifio Railway, however, runs no risk of losing its well won laurels.
So the ' Witness,' a faithful organ of the Liberal party, has criticised this undertaking, and that shows that the people had not been sufficiently enlightened at its outset in 1903.
It is contended that the people have approved of this undertaking. The people in this country are sometimes consulted in odd fashion; that is they are consulted after the matter has gone through, and not at all before it is decided and the contracts awarded. The people are fooled, and later on the government boasts of having obtained their approval. As I have already said, there are two ways of consulting the people, before or after deciding. It seems to me it would be more manly and fairer on the part of the government to consult the people before taking their decision, instead of waiting until that decision has been taken. For instance, in the case of that undertaking, which was launched towards the end of the parliament of 1900, it would have been a very easy matter indeed to submit it to the electorate at the election of 1904, previous to starting the work.
In connection with the increase of the salaries of the ministers and members of parliament the proposal was brought forward immediately after the general election of 1904, although the people had not had the least inkling of it in the course of the elections. It seems as though the people had approved that measure, but in that case again they accepted a state of things already in existence.
In regard to this important proposal for the granting of an amount of $10,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, it would have been an easy matter to submit it to the people at the last general elections. But nothing of the sort has been done. It would have been necessary to enlighten the people, to acquaint them with the facts and circumstances; but it was thought preferable to leave them under the false impression of 1904.

speechtext:
In answer to that question, I may say that, had I been here I would have voted against that proposal, not so much because I considered it unfair in itself, but on account of its being sprung by surprise on the people. I am not called upon to discuss that question just now; I have referred to it by the way and not with any idea of criticism. It seems to me that in connection with questions of such importance, it would be advisable to consult the people. The manner of consulting the people which the government have adopted is not the ideal one to my mind. It is in accordance neither with the spirit nor with the letter of the constitution. It is an arbitrary and antiliberal mode of procedure; it is neither generous nor frank, and surely it is not manly.
That sovereign people in whose presence, during the elections, politicians are so apt to take a cringing attitude, is deserving of more consideration.
As will have been noticed, the extra expenditure on this undertaking will be enormous. As stated by the ' Witness ' that road will entail on the Dominion an expenditure, not of thirteen millions, not of a hundred millions, but rather of $250,000,000 or possibly $280,000,000. This government is going to supply all the funds for this undertaking from Moncton to Prince Rupert, from ocean to ocean, for all sections east and west, and the prairie and mountain sub-sections, including the Quebec bridge, and these amounts will be returned when there are funds available.
With whom are we dealing? Is it with the Grand Trunk Pacific, or with the Grand Trunk Company of Canada, or with a third company which has made its appearance under the name of the Grand Trunk Town Site and Development Company; or lastly, is it with the fourth company, the "Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Line Company"? All these companies are apparently amalgamated ; the directors are the same in every case, they constitute in reality a single moral person; and I say that parliament should under the circumstances show great caution in granting them favours. They are endeavouring to secure privileges, while avoiding all risks. These companies are much more anxious to make money out of us than to endure the welfare of the country.
The hon. Minister of Railways stated a minute ago how important it was from our point of view to have an entirely Canadian line of railway, over an all-Canadin route. Now, do all these companies which seem so anxious to provide us with an all-Canadian Mr. ETHIER.
Transcontinental Railway, have as stock holders and directors Canadian citizens, oi at any rate foreigners intending to become citizens of Canada. Are they not rather strangers, Americans, anxious to make money at our expense, without even going to the length of getting naturalized?
When I heard the Minister of Railways and his friends booming the West, I remember what the Liberals had to say in this connection in 1880 and 1884. It is important, I think, to recall the past, for fear certain incidents in the history of our country should be too soon consigned to oblivion. It was not usual then to boom the West, to speak of it as destined to become the world's great storehouse. I shall quote presently some of the sayings of these gentlemen in that connection, when the Canadian Pacific Railway was applying to parliament for help towards the completion of their undertaking.
However, as regards this proposed second transcontinental, it was launched prematurely, with inexplicable haste, in the full blast of a session, when parliament was drawing to an end, and against all expectations. It should be no matter for surprise if in the end the expenditure is found to be enormous. Arrangements were taken as if the matter had been of very little importance, without going to the pains of getting precise information in regard to the physical features of the country through which the railway was to be built, nor as regards the expenditure, and the cost of the road in stead of amounting to $13,000 per mile or $30,000 per mile, reaches $35,000 and even $80,000 per mile.
That is not surprising; it was bound to happen, and the best evidence of it I find in a speech of the right hon. Prime Minister, delivered on July 30th, 1903. He said:
I do not expect even the most fastidious of our critics will ask us that we should have had an exploration across the prairies. They are satisfied that we have enough information now to deal with this question so far as the prairies are concerned. But I shall be asked: What about the Rocky mountains? My answer in regard to the Rocky mountains is that we have mountains of information. We have mountains of books, pamphlets and reports-books, pamphlets and reports from traders, from explorers, from engineers.
And he mentioned Samuel de Champlain, Robert Cavelier de la Salle, La Verendyre, Alexander Mackenzie, Captain Butler and many others who at that early date, in their travels on land and sea, had not the least idea of making surveys or specifications and estimates for railways. No wonder that with such data, the government should have been out in their calculations.
